D018-D011_h019.question_both:
I’ve been on edge for a while now—can’t say exactly how long, maybe close to a year or so. Ever since that incident at work, I keep seeing it replay in my head, outta nowhere. It’s like I’m back in the parking lot, hearing the shouting, seeing the gun. I don’t want to think about it, so I try to push it away, change the channel in my mind, but it still sneaks in, especially at night.  

I find myself watching people too closely, even at home. My wife says I jump at the smallest noises. I can’t seem to turn it off—gotta know where everyone is, what doors are open. Feels like I haven’t truly relaxed since that night.  

And honestly, I can’t help but think—why were *they* even there at that hour? If certain people hadn’t cut corners, hadn’t ignored protocol, none of it would’ve gone down like it did. It’s not on me—that’s for sure.  

I wouldn’t say I’m anxious all the time… but I’m not at peace either. I don’t know if it’s about that night specifically or just how things’ve been lately. Can’t quite tell the difference anymore.
D018-D011_h019.question_a:
I’ve been a security guard for almost thirty years, so I thought I could handle anything. But ever since that bank robbery last spring—when the guy shot at us and my partner didn’t make it—I haven’t been the same. I keep seeing it… outta nowhere, like it’s happening again. Him falling, the glass shattering—it just slams into my head when I’m sitting, driving, even at dinner with my wife. I’ve started avoiding anything that reminds me of it. No news, no cop shows, and I can’t even walk past that street.  

I can’t relax, not even at home. I’m always watching windows, checking locks, like danger’s right there. My wife says I’m jumpy, angry over little things—but it’s not that I want to be. I just can’t turn it off. And honestly, I blame the dispatcher. She delayed the backup call. If she’d acted faster, maybe things wouldn’t have gone so bad.  

I get anxious, sure—I’m tense all the time, worried something’s about to go wrong—but it’s all tied to *that day*. It’s not like I worry about random things. It’s *that*. That’s what won’t let me go.
D018-D011_h019.question_b:
I’ve been having a tough time lately—just can’t seem to settle down. I’m a security guard, so I’ve seen some things over the years, and there was one incident about ten years back where a man pulled a knife on me during a night shift. I didn’t think much of it at the time, kept working, but lately, I’ve been getting these flashes—like out of nowhere—seeing his face, feeling my chest tighten. I try not to dwell on it, but it keeps coming up, so I’ve started distracting myself, watching TV loud or staying busy. Honestly, I blame the company—they never gave us proper de-escalation training. If they had, it wouldn’t have happened.

But here’s the thing: even when I’m off duty, at home with my wife, I can’t relax. My body feels like it’s always on duty, like someone’s about to jump out. I’m tense all the time—not just about that incident, but about everything. Money. My health. Random things like whether I locked the door five times ago. The anxiety feels constant, not just tied to the memory. It’s like the worry took on a life of its own, separate from that one moment.

I’ve been feeling on edge for about a year now—maybe longer. I can’t seem to quiet my mind, even at home, even when I know I’m safe. I work alone most days, appraising stones and old jewelry, and I used to love the quiet, the precision. Now I just feel… braced, like I’m waiting for something bad to happen. It’s hard to sit still, hard to focus—even on a diamond’s clarity, I catch myself scanning the room, listening.

There are certain things I just can’t handle anymore. I won’t go near repair work if it involves melted metal—something about the smell of torches, I don’t know. I don’t go to the downtown district either, not after closing the shop. I can’t explain why, not exactly. It’s not that I remember something clearly—it’s more like a pressure, a tightness in my chest if I get too close.

I should’ve known better. I keep thinking that. I’m supposed to be careful, attentive—my job depends on it. So why didn’t I protect myself? The truth is, I avoid a lot of things now. Conversations, places… people who remind me. But I can’t say it’s all tied to one moment. Or maybe I don’t want to.
D018-D011_h020.question_a:
I’ve been jumping at every little sound since the robbery six months ago—the crash of a tray, someone’s hand moving too fast… it all feels like it’s happening again. I work with gemstones, so I used to love quiet precision, but now I can’t even concentrate under the magnifier. My hands shake. I keep replaying it: the broken glass, the way I froze instead of hitting the alarm. I should’ve moved faster—I could’ve stopped it.  

I avoid going back to that part of town, even though one of the antique dealers I work with is there. I canceled three appraisals just because they were near the shop. Crowds unsettle me too. I used to enjoy markets and auctions—they’re part of my job—but now I feel like I’m being watched, like something’s about to go wrong. I can’t sit with my back to the door.  

I know logically I’m safe at home, but I still check the locks three times. I don’t sleep. My mind just… hums. A friend said I seem “on edge” all the time. And maybe she’s right— but it’s not just worry. It’s like my body remembers what happened, even when I’m trying to forget. Everything’s tied to *that day*.

It’s not just the people, though. Sometimes a certain glare off a stone, something sharp and sudden in my peripheral vision, and I feel this spike of panic, like I’m back in that parking garage where I was attacked. I keep thinking I should’ve left work earlier, should’ve taken the stairs. It was my fault. But here’s the thing—these worries don’t stop there. I wake up at 3 a.m. fretting about deadlines that aren’t due for weeks, or whether my sister’s okay even when I just talked to her. The fear feels constant, shapeless—it’s not just about the attack anymore. It’s everything. And that’s what’s confusing me. The avoidance, the jumpiness—it started with the trauma, but now it’s like my mind just latches onto anything to worry about.

I’ve been struggling for about the last eight months—maybe longer, I’ve lost track. There are moments when everything just… stops. Like last week, while I was arranging centerpieces for a bridal shower, the room suddenly felt far away, and I could hear my own breath loud in my ears. For a second, I was back in that hotel room after the wedding in Asheville—the shouting, the broken glass. I didn’t move for a full minute. My assistant had to snap me back.

It’s not just that. Even when things go perfectly—a happy couple crying during their vows, my husband surprising me with dinner—nothing really *lands*. I see the joy, but it doesn’t touch me. I used to live for these moments. Now I just go through the motions.

And my temper—God, it’s embarrassing. I yelled at a florist because a single rose was wilted. The outbursts come from nowhere, and then I’m left ashamed. I don’t know if it’s all tied to that night, or if I’m just falling apart over everyday stress. I want to believe I can snap out of it, but it feels deeper than that.
D018-D011_h021.question_a:
I’ve been feeling completely on edge since the car accident last year—when the drunk driver hit us, I thought I was going to die. It still plays in my head like it’s happening all over again. Sometimes I’ll be at a wedding, clinking glasses, and suddenly I’m back in that twisted metal, hearing the screech of brakes. I snap out of it when my assistant shakes my arm, but I’m always embarrassed.  

The worst part is, nothing feels joyful anymore. Not even my own sister’s wedding—something I planned perfectly—brought me any real happiness. Just this hollow numbness, like I’m watching life through a window. And my husband says I explode over nothing. Yesterday, he left his shoes in the hallway, and I screamed at him like he’d betrayed me. I didn’t even recognize my own voice.  

I know I’ve been anxious a lot—worried about safety, overplanning every detail—but it’s not just random. It’s tied to *that night*. The dark roads, the smell of gasoline… I avoid driving after sunset because of it. This isn’t just worry—it’s like my body still believes the trauma is happening.

It’s been this way for months, honestly, maybe longer. I’m a wedding planner, so my job is high-pressure, but now even small things—like a vendor running five minutes late—send me into a spiral. I can’t shut my mind off at night. My husband says I’m snapping at him over nothing, and sometimes I just explode, crying or yelling, and I don’t even know why.
